text: Thirty-eight years later, it went bankrupt, best known for asking you for your phone number when you bought one of these.
I'm Sam. This is Last Receipt. Tonight, why RadioShack failed, and how it had the future and sold batteries instead.
Every kid who liked taking things apart grew up in that store. Resistors in little drawers. Kits that turned into radios. It was the place where you learned how things worked.
Now watch this. RadioShack had the stores, the brand and the customers who would build the computer age. The kids in those aisles became the engineers.
RadioShack just didn't build anything for them.
Why does a store need your phone number to sell you a nine-volt? Everyone asked. Nobody liked it.
And by then, RadioShack had pushed most of the parts drawers into a corner to make room for phone cases.
Here's the thing about a name. It's only worth what it promises. When the promise is gone, you're just selling the letters.
So what killed RadioShack? Amazon, partly. Big-box stores, partly. Phones, definitely.
But here's my verdict. RadioShack's real customers were the curious ones. The builders. It had them first, and it kept trading them for whatever was selling that year.
The lesson: know who your weirdest, most loyal customers are. They're usually a few years ahead of everyone else.
What did you build with something from RadioShack? Tell me in the comments. I want to hear about the kits.
